Since He promised him this great promise, He reminded him of His blessings upon him during his upbringing. ﴿Did He not find you﴾ (yaʿlamka: know you) ﴿an orphan﴾: his father died, peace be upon him, while he was still in the womb, and six months after that his mother died, peace be upon her, when he was eight years old. His paternal uncle Abū Ṭālib then took charge of him and raised him well. It was said to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq: Why did the Prophet (ﷺ) lose both his parents? He said: So that no created being would have a claim upon him.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: As for those who claim that the interpretation is from the expression "a unique pearl" (durrah yatīmah), meaning: did He not find you unique among the Quraysh, without equal, and so He gave you shelter? End of quote. The majority read *fa-āwā* in the four-letter form. Abū al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī read *fa-awā* in the three-letter form, meaning "had mercy," as in: "I showed mercy to so-and-so," i.e. you had mercy on him. From this is the line of the poet:

"I see myself, and by Allah, there is no ingratitude, that I have asked my own self for something that does not grant it."

﴿And He found you lost﴾: it cannot be taken to mean the straying that is the opposite of guidance, because the prophets are protected from that. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it means his straying in his childhood in the ravines of Mecca, after which Allah returned him to his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. It was also said that his straying was from his wet-nurse Ḥalīma. It was also said that he went astray on the road to Syria when Abū Ṭālib took him out. Some exegetes have views in which there is something that is impermissible to attribute to the prophets, peace be upon them. I saw in a dream that I was reflecting on this sentence, and I immediately said: "And He found you" means He found your people "lost," so He guided them through you. Then I said: this is by omitting a noun, as in: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yūsuf 82].

The majority read *ʿāʾilan* ("in need"), i.e. poor. Jarīr said:

"Allah revealed in the Book an obligation for the wayfarer and for the poor person in need."

It is repeated for variation in wording. Al-Yamānī read *ʿayyilan*, like *sayyid*, with a doubled, kasra-vowelled *yāʾ*. From this is the line of Uḥayḥa ibn al-Ḥallāj:

"The poor man does not know when he will become rich, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor."

*ʿāla* means he became poor; *aʿāla* means his dependants increased. Muqātil said: ﴿and enriched you﴾ means your contentment with what He gave you of provision. It was also said: He made you rich through contentment and patience. It was also said: through sufficiency.

When He enumerated these three blessings to him, He charged him with three things that correspond to them. ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾: Mujāhid said: do not despise him. Ibn Sallām said: do not cause him to slip. Sufyān said: do not wrong him by wasting his property. Al-Farrā' said: do not withhold his right. *Al-qahr* is domination that causes harm. The majority read *taqhar* with *qāf*, while Ibn Masʿūd and Ibrāhīm al-Taymī read it with *kāf* in place of *qāf*, which is a dialect form with the same meaning as the majority reading.

﴿And as for the one who asks﴾: its apparent meaning is the one who seeks help ﴿do not repulse him﴾, i.e. do not rebuke him. However, give to him, or turn him away with kind words. Qatāda said: do not be harsh with him. This corresponds to ﴿and He found you in need and enriched you﴾. So "the one who asks," as we have said, is the one who seeks help. This was said by al-Farrā' and a group of others. Abū al-Dardā', al-Ḥasan and others said: [p. 487] "the one who asks" here means the one who asks about knowledge and religion, not the one who asks for money. This would correspond to ﴿and He found you lost and guided you﴾.

﴿And as for the favour of your Lord, proclaim it﴾. Mujāhid and al-Kalbī said: its meaning is: spread the Qur'an and convey what you were sent with. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: it is prophethood. Others said: it is general, covering all blessings. Al-Zamakhsharī said: proclaiming the blessings means thanking for them and making them known, meaning the blessings he mentioned: shelter, guidance, enrichment, and whatever else. End of quote. It seems that, since the mention of the favour upon him was made by naming three things, He commanded him with three things: He mentioned the orphan first, which is the starting point, then He mentioned the one who asks second, which is the one in need. The most noble of what He favoured him with was guidance, so He ascended from these two to the more noble and made it the conclusion of the surah. He placed this in the middle when mentioning the three things because after the orphan comes the time of obligation, and he, peace be upon him, was protected from committing anything that displeases Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in speech, action or belief. So the mention of the favour in this respect follows the reality after the orphanhood and the state of obligation. In the other case, He ascended to the more noble, so these are two aims of the address.
